A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the enzyme-distributed model of lidocaine metabolism is superior to the “well-stired” and “parallel tube” models for the low input concentrations of lidocaine (1.5–2 μg/ml or 6–8 μM) and MEGX (2.3–4.6 μg/ml or about 9–18 μM) in the once-through, retrograde and normal flow perfusion studies.
the enzyme-distributed models for lidocaine and its metabolites appear to be superior to evenly distributed systems and “well-stired” models for predicting hepatic availability.

the distribution of N-dealkylation and hydroxy lation activities for lidocine metabolism is not even or parallel, and the enzyme-distributed models for lidocaine and lidocaine metabolite metabolism are more consistent with the experimental data than the “parallel tube,” “well-stir red,” or “parallel tube-well-stirred” composite models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distribution of enzyme activities is a major determinant of drug clearance.

a model of lidocaine metabolism based on an enzyme-distributed system is superior to the “well-stired” model and “parallel tube” models in predicting the hepatic availability of both lidocaine and its metabolites.
the distribution of enzymic activities in liver parenchyma may be an important factor to consider in the design of in vitro systems for drug metabolism and pharmacokinetic studies.
